SECTION A: INITIATION & ADMISSION OF CIRP  
1. Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd., (2017) 1 SCC 407  
IBC 2016 Sections: 5(7)-(8), 5(21), 7 (Financial creditor definition and initiation)  
Facts: Innoventive Industries faced financial difficulties and entered into a Master Restructuring  
Agreement (MRA) with creditors including ICICI Bank to restructure debt with moratorium period.  
After the restructuring period, when the company failed to make payments, ICICI Bank initiated  
CIRP proceedings under Section 7 IBC on ground of default of financial debt. Innoventive  
challenged the initiation, arguing: (1) No unconditional debt existed; (2) Payment obligations were  
subject to creditors infusing funds; (3) Restructuring moratorium prevented default claim. NCLT  
admitted petition; Innoventive appealed.  
Held: The Supreme Court upheld CIRP initiation and established landmark doctrine of financial  
creditor definition and default. The Court held: (1) Financial debt includes obligations to  
infuse funds, even if time value is embedded in restructuring; (2) Default means non-  
payment of financial debt, regardless of underlying conditions; (3) Payment obligations under  
MRA are unconditional creditors' counter-obligations (funding infusion) are separate and don't  
prevent debtor's payment default; (4) Financial creditor can initiate CIRP without needing to  
prove default by 14 additional days mere non-payment within 180 days after communication  
suffices; (5) IBC is creditor-friendly framework courts won't prevent creditors from exercising  
rights. This established doctrine of creditor-friendly interpretation.  
2. Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India, (2019) 14 SCC 491  
IBC 2016 Sections: 5(8), 7, 21 (Financial creditors - real estate allottees)  
Facts: Pioneer Urban Land, a real estate developer, developed multiple housing projects and  
faced financial crisis unable to deliver promised units. Homebuyers (allottees) who had paid  
significant amounts (50-90% of consideration) applied to initiate CIRP against the developer  
under Section 7, claiming status as "financial creditors." Developer contended: (1) Allottees are  
operational creditors (service provision); (2) Real estate transactions are not financial debts; (3)  
Money received is advance payment for goods/services, not loan. NCLT admitted petition;  
developer challenged before Supreme Court.  
Held: The Supreme Court recognized homebuyers as financial creditors for real estate  
advance payments. The judgment held: (1) Advance payment by allottee = financial  
debt (debtor receives funds upfront but delivers after months/years); (2) Time value of money  
exists allottee advances funds for months before receiving property; (3) Recognition justified  
protects homebuyer interests in insolvency; (4) Financial creditor status gives voting rights in  
Committee of Creditors; (5) However, distinction: genuine allottees qualify; speculative  
investors/traders don't. This established doctrine of homebuyer protection in real estate  
insolvency.

3. Amit Katyal v. Anand Rathi Global Finance Pvt. Ltd., (2022) 136 Taxmann 55 (SC)  
IBC 2016 Sections: 7, 8, 9 (Financial vs operational creditor distinction)  
Facts: A builder (corporate debtor) undertook housing project but failed to complete it within 8  
years, causing severe losses and hardship to homebuyers who had paid amounts. Three  
homebuyers filed petition under Section 7 claiming financial creditor status for amounts paid  
toward property purchase (not loan). The builder argued: (1) These are supply contracts (goods  
property), hence operational debt; (2) Distinction between advance payment for goods vs financial  
debt. NCLT admitted petition treating allottees as financial creditors.  
Held: The Supreme Court upheld financial creditor status for homebuyers reaffirming Pioneer  
Urban Land principle. The judgment emphasized: (1) Substance over form real estate advance  
payments are financial debts despite being for goods delivery; (2) Financial debt definition  
includes debt which is disbursed against consideration for time value of money; (3) Allottee  
advances funds knowing delivery will occur months later this time lag creates financial debt  
character; (4) Policy rationale: Homebuyer protection in real estate crisis; (5) Creditor-friendly  
interpretation of definitions. However, speculative investors with no possession intent  
excluded. This reinforced doctrine of homebuyer protection.  
SECTION B: RESOLUTION PROCESS & CoC ROLE  
4. Sundaresh Bhatt, Liquidator of ABG Shipyard v. Central Board of Indirect Taxes &  
Customs, (2022) 2 SCC 595  
IBC 2016 Sections: 14 (Moratorium), 33 (Liquidation and moratorium continuation)  
Facts: ABG Shipyard entered CIRP but no successful resolution plan emerged; liquidation was  
ordered. During liquidation, imported goods (warehouse-stored) were subject to customs duties  
demand by Central Board of Indirect Taxes & Customs (CBIIC). CBIIC sought to recover customs  
duties from the company and claim warehoused goods. The liquidator argued: (1) Moratorium  
under IBC 14 continues during liquidation; (2) CBIIC cannot proceed with duty collection during  
moratorium; (3) IBC provisions prevail over Customs Act. CBIIC contended customs duties are  
distinct from insolvency debt and cannot be stayed.  
Held: The Supreme Court upheld moratorium continuation during liquidation and held  
that IBC prevails over other laws (Customs Act, Excise Act, etc.). The Court held: (1) Section  
33(5) IBC: Moratorium continues even after liquidation order; (2) All legal proceedings  
suspended against corporate debtor, including customs/excise recovery; (3) No multiplicity of  
suits IBC framework controls; (4) Liquidator has custodial rights over all assets including  
warehoused goods; (5) Statutory duties (customs, taxes) are claims in liquidation, not separate  
proceedings. This established doctrine of moratorium supremacy and IBC supremacy over  
other laws.  
5. Independent Sugar Corporation Ltd. v. Hindustan National Gas & Industries Ltd., (2025)  
SCC OnLine SC 23  
3
IBC, 2016  
IBC 2016 Sections: 31(4), proviso (CCI approval requirement for resolution plans)  
Facts: A resolution plan was submitted in CIRP proposing acquisition by a resolution applicant  
(SRA) which would constitute "combination" under Competition Act 2002  
a
(merger/consolidation). The Committee of Creditors (CoC) approved the plan without obtaining  
prior approval from Competition Commission of India (CCI). SRA sought NCLT approval; NCLT  
granted it. Later, CCI issued notice questioning whether the combination was approved by CCI  
before CoC approval, arguing it must obtain CCI approval. Question arose: Must CCI approve  
BEFORE CoC votes, or can approval be sought after CoC approval?  
Held: The Supreme Court held that Section 31(4) proviso makes CCI approval MANDATORY  
and must be PRIOR to CoC approval. The judgment established: (1) "Prior approval" means  
CCI must approve BEFORE CoC votes; (2) Proviso is mandatory cannot be waived or  
overlooked; (3) Rationale: CCI may approve, reject, or impose conditions on combination CoC  
must vote with this knowledge; (4) Non-compliance renders plan legally unsustainable even  
if CoC approves; (5) Courts cannot create exceptions to mandatory statutory requirements.  
This established doctrine of mandatory CCI approval for combinations in IBC.  
6. Kalyani Transco Pvt. Ltd. v. Bhushan Power & Steel Ltd., (2025) SCC OnLine SC 1010  
IBC 2016 Sections: 12 (CIRP timelines), 30-31 (Plan approval conditions), 33 (Implementation  
timelines)  
Facts: Bhushan Power & Steel's CIRP extended beyond 330 days (maximum timeline under IBC  
including extensions). A resolution plan was approved and submitted to NCLT, but SRA failed to  
implement plan within stipulated timelines. When pressed for implementation, SRA sought further  
extensions on grounds of market conditions and funding constraints. Creditors argued: (1) 330-  
day timeline is absolute; (2) No extensions beyond 330 days permissible; (3) Non-implementation  
should trigger liquidation.  
Held: The Supreme Court enforced strict 330-day timeline for CIRP (180 days + 150 days  
extension maximum, per Section 12). The judgment held: (1) 330-day limit is absolute and  
cannot be extended further; (2) Delays beyond 330 days defeat IBC's objective of expeditious  
resolution; (3) If CIRP cannot complete within 330 days, Liquidation must follow (Section 33);  
(4) Implementation of approved plan must commence immediately; (5) Moratorium cannot  
be extended indefinitely its purpose is temporary to give breathing space, not indefinite relief.  
This established doctrine of strict timeline enforcement in IBC.  
SECTION C: RESOLUTION PLAN IMPLEMENTATION & WITHDRAWAL  
7. Jet Airways (India) Ltd. CIRP - Supreme Court Order, (2024) SCC OnLine SC 1194  
IBC 2016 Sections: 12, 30, 30(2), 31, 33 (Plan conditions and implementation)  
Facts: Jet Airways entered CIRP in June 2019. Jalan Kalrock Consortium emerged as successful  
resolution applicant (SRA). CoC approved plan; NCLT approved on June 22, 2021. However,  
SRA failed to meet conditions precedent (CPs) as stipulated including payments, regulatory  
4
IBC, 2016  
approvals, and operational preparations. SRA claimed CPs were "substantially complied" and  
sought extensions and PBG (Performance Bank Guarantee) adjustment. Despite non-  
compliance, NCLT and NCLAT allowed continued operations, granting waivers to SRA. After  
years of delay, Jet Airways remained grounded. Creditors (lenders) appealed to Supreme Court.  
Held: The Supreme Court ordered liquidation of Jet Airways finding repeated plan non-  
implementation. The judgment held: (1) Conditions Precedent must be fully complied, not  
"substantially" no partial compliance; (2) SRA cannot modify plan terms or claim CPs are  
waived without creditor consent; (3) NCLAT cannot allow PBG adjustments contrary to plan  
terms and Court's prior directions; (4) Effective date of plan cannot commence until all CPs are  
met; (5) Court described case as "eye-opener" highlighting NCLT/NCLAT shortcomings in  
enforcing plan discipline. This established doctrine of strict plan compliance and  
implementation.  
8. Velu Chairman, Monitoring Committee v. Invent Assets Securitisation & Reconstruction  
Pvt. Ltd., (2021) SCC Online NCLAT 1203  
IBC 2016 Sections: 31, 33 (Plan approval and liquidation post-failure)  
Facts: A resolution plan was approved by CoC and NCLT for Palm Lagoon Backwater Resorts.  
However, SRA failed to implement the approved plan and was unable to infuse promised funds  
and complete operational revival. After expiry of implementation timelines, stakeholders  
approached the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) seeking liquidation order arguing plan  
implementation had failed.  
Held: NCLAT (affirmed judicial principle) held that: (1) If SRA fails to implement plan, NCLT  
can pass liquidation order under Section 33; (2) Non-implementation of approved plan is  
sufficient ground for liquidation; (3) NCLT is NOT functus officio after plan approval it can  
exercise Section 33 powers to liquidate if implementation fails; (4) Court can invoke Section  
60(5) to recall its plan approval order if implementation becomes impossible; (5) Liquidation  
becomes inevitable when resolution plan fails implementation. This established doctrine of  
liquidation as consequence of failed resolution.  
SECTION D: CREDITOR CLASSIFICATION & PRIORITIES  
9. DBS Bank Limited Singapore v. Ruchi Soya Industries Limited, (2024) 1 SCC 1  
IBC 2016 Sections: 5(21) (Operational creditor definition), 8 (Operational creditor petition), 9  
(Verification of claim)  
Facts: DBS Bank extended financial debt of Rs. 243 crores to Ruchi Soya. Under credit  
agreement, DBS Bank provided overdraft facility and other banking services. Ruchi Soya  
defaulted on payments. DBS Bank filed CIRP petition under Section 7 (financial creditor). Ruchi  
Soya contested arguing: (1) DBS Bank's claim is mixed partially financial, partially operational  
(banking services); (2) Cannot be pure financial creditor claim. Question arose: How to classify  
mixed claims where both financial and operational elements exist?  
5
IBC, 2016  
Held: The Supreme Court held that debt characterization depends on substance, not form.  
The judgment established: (1) Primary character of debt is determinative; (2) If debt is  
fundamentally financial (borrowing) with incidental services, treat as financial debt; (3) Set-off  
rights apply creditor can deduct amounts it owes to debtor from amount debtor owes to creditor;  
(4) No double recovery net claim after set-off is operative; (5) Financial creditor status is  
determined by principal obligation, not ancillary services. This established doctrine of  
substantive characterization of debt.  
10. Mansi Brar Fernandes v. Union of India, (2021) SCC Online SC 1098  
IBC 2016 Sections: 5(8), 7, 29A (Financial creditor - speculative investors exclusion)  
Facts: A speculative real estate investor purchased multiple property units with minimal  
investment expecting resale profit. When real estate market declined, investor filed petition under  
Section 7 claiming "financial creditor" status (advance payment for property) to trigger CIRP  
against developer as debt recovery mechanism. Developer challenged arguing investor is  
speculative trader, not genuine allottee. Question: Can speculative investors use IBC as collection  
mechanism?  
Held: The Supreme Court clarified speculative investors CANNOT use IBC and distinguished  
genuine allottees from speculative investors. The judgment held: (1) Genuine allottee test: Must  
have genuine intent to take possession of property; (2) Speculative investor: Purchasing units  
only for profit with no possession intent; (3) IBC is not debt recovery mechanism for  
speculative/trading claims; (4) Distinction through examination: Court must examine buyer's  
intent, purpose, profile; (5) Speculative investors excluded from financial creditor status. This  
established doctrine of genuine allottee identification vs speculative investor exclusion.  
SECTION E: MORATORIUM & STATUTORY PROTECTIONS  
11. ABG Shipyard Liquidation v. CBIC (Customs), (2022) 2 SCC 595  
IBC 2016 Sections: 14 (Moratorium), 21 (Suspension of prosecution), 33(5) (Moratorium  
continuation in liquidation)  
Facts: During ABG Shipyard's liquidation, Central Board of Indirect Taxes & Customs (CBIC)  
sought to recover custom duties alleged to be owed by the company for imported goods stored  
in warehouses. CBIC initiated recovery proceedings separate from insolvency. Liquidator argued:  
(1) Moratorium under Section 14 prohibits separate proceedings; (2) Moratorium continues even  
in liquidation; (3) All claims must be processed through liquidation, not separate recovery.  
Held: The Supreme Court upheld moratorium supremacy and held: (1) Section 14  
moratorium covers all legal proceedings including customs recovery; (2) Section 33(5):  
Moratorium continues during liquidation; (3) IBC is a comprehensive code prevails over  
Customs Act, Excise Act, PMLA; (4) No parallel proceedings can be initiated during moratorium;  
(5) Statutory dues (taxes, duties) are claims in insolvency process, not separate proceedings.  
This established doctrine of moratorium as absolute bar to parallel proceedings.  
6
IBC, 2016  
12. Section 32A Immunity v. Criminal Prosecution - IBC Jurisprudence  
IBC 2016 Sections: 32A (Limited immunity for successful resolution applicant)  
Facts: After a resolution plan was approved and SRA took over the company, certain  
creditors/stakeholders raised concerns that the corporate debtor (now controlled by SRA) should  
not benefit from past criminal conduct by former management. Former management (promoters)  
had allegedly engaged in criminal fraud, misappropriation, or regulatory violations. Question  
arose: Does Section 32A immunity shield SRA/corporate debtor from consequences of past  
criminal misconduct?  
Held: Supreme Court jurisprudence clarified that Section 32A provides LIMITED immunity.  
The judgment established: (1) Section 32A shields CORPORATE DEBTOR (post-resolution)  
from pre-resolution liabilities/claims; (2) DOES NOT shield individuals who committed criminal  
misconduct; (3) Criminal prosecution of promoters/past management continues unaffected;  
(4) Individuals remain accountable for criminal conduct; (5) Purpose of Section 32A: Ring-  
fence company for revival, not exonerate criminals. This established doctrine of limited Section  
32A immunity with criminal accountability preserved.  
SECTION F: LIQUIDATION & ASSET REALIZATION  
13. R.K. Industries (Unit-II) LLP v. HR Commercials Pvt. Ltd., (2022) 7 SCC 204  
IBC 2016 Sections: 238 (Liquidation and asset vesting), 240 (Liquidator powers), 241 (Sale of  
assets)  
Facts: ABG Shipyard's liquidation involved sale of assets. Liquidator decided to adopt "Swiss  
Challenge" process (two-stage bidding) and sale by private treaty rather than open auction. R.K.  
Industries emerged as anchor bidder in first stage but subsequently liquidator cancelled the Swiss  
Challenge process and decided to sell asset to another bidder through different process. R.K.  
Industries challenged liquidator's decision arguing it had unfair withdrawal of opportunity.  
Held: The Supreme Court upheld liquidator's commercial discretion in asset sale. The  
judgment held: (1) Liquidator has complete discretion on mode and method of asset sale to  
maximize value; (2) SCC recommendations are advisory, not binding on liquidator;  
(3) Liquidator can modify/cancel sale process if better realization possible; (4) Judicial  
review limited to arbitrariness or bad faith; (5) Commercial wisdom of liquidator is  
protected courts won't substitute business decisions. This established doctrine of liquidator  
autonomy in asset sale decisions.  
14. Arcelor Mittal India Pvt. Ltd. v. Satish Kumar Gupta, (2019) 4 SCC 430  
IBC 2016 Sections: 29A (Eligibility conditions for resolution applicants), 39 (Resolution applicant  
qualifications)  
Facts: Arcelor Mittal India Pvt. Ltd. sought eligibility to bid for acquisition of a company  
undergoing CIRP. However, Arcelor's promoter had history of financial defaults and was subject  
7
IBC, 2016  
to Section 29A IBC disqualification. The company argued: (1) Past defaults are historic; (2)  
Current financial position is strong; (3) Section 29A bars should not apply retroactively. NCLT and  
NCLAT allowed bidding; case reached Supreme Court.  
Held: The Supreme Court strictly upheld Section 29A disqualifications. The judgment held:  
(1) Section 29A disqualifications are absolute and cannot be waived; (2) No exceptions to  
statutory prohibitions; (3) Policy rationale: Prevent promoters with default history from acquiring  
same company; (4) Disqualifications apply even after debt settlement; (5) NCLT/NCLAT  
cannot grant exceptions to statutory eligibility conditions. This established doctrine of  
mandatory Section 29A disqualifications.  
15. Mohammed Enterprises (Tanzania) Ltd. v. Farooq Ali Khan & Ors., (2025) SCC OnLine  
SC 23  
IBC 2016 Sections: 15, 61, 226 (High Court writ jurisdiction in IBC)  
Facts: A resolution plan was approved by CoC and NCLT but later challenged in High Court  
under Article 226 writ jurisdiction claiming violation of natural justice. The High Court entertained  
the writ petition and annulled the CoC-approved plan. Aggrieved by High Court's interference,  
case reached Supreme Court. The question was: Whether High Courts should exercise writ  
jurisdiction in matters governed by IBC where comprehensive statutory remedies exist?  
Held: The Supreme Court held that IBC is self-contained code with its own remedies and High  
Courts must exercise extreme caution. The judgment held: (1) IBC provides complete  
appellate mechanism (NCLAT from NCLT, Supreme Court from NCLAT); (2) High Court writ  
jurisdiction should not interfere with IBC proceedings; (3) Exhaustion of statutory remedies  
required before High Court jurisdiction; (4) Finality and timeliness of CIRP essential to IBC's  
success; (5) High Court interference undermines IBC objectives. This established doctrine  
of IBC as self-contained code with limited writ jurisdiction.
